column1: What is the AdvoKC BAT-O-METER?
column2: The AdvoKC Foundation's tracker of Tinubu's campaign promises; its third-year report was published on 3 June 2026.

column1: What were AdvoKC's third-year ratings?
column2: Of 53 promises: 11 kept (20.8%), 22 compromised (41.5%) and 20 broken (37.7%).

column1: What is the difference between a "Compromised" and a "Broken" rating?
column2: Compromised means some progress but delivery falls short; Broken means the commitment is considered unfulfilled.

column1: Which sector did AdvoKC rate strongest?
column2: Education: 3 of 4 promises kept (student loans, new curriculum, reduced ASUU strike disruption); university autonomy was compromised.

column1: How did the economy sector score in the BAT-O-METER?
column2: 31 of the 53 promises: 8 kept, 13 compromised and 10 broken.

column1: Give examples of promises AdvoKC rated broken.
column2: Ending estimated electricity billing, eliminating kidnapping, reviving Ajaokuta Steel, completing major rail projects and environmental restoration.

column1: What is the Renewed Hope manifesto?
column2: Renewed Hope 2023: Action Plan for a Better Nigeria, the 80-page APC manifesto published on 21 October 2022.

column1: What is the difference between AdvoKC's 53 promises and OpenPolls' 88 commitments?
column2: They are separate datasets: AdvoKC rated a 53-promise sample; OpenPolls extracted 88 commitments from the manifesto. Their denominators must not be mixed.

column1: What law established the student loan fund (NELFUND)?
column2: The Student Loans (Access to Higher Education) Act 2024.

column1: What evidence supports the "new curriculum" promise?
column2: A revised Basic and Senior Secondary curriculum was released in September 2025 for the 2025/2026 school year; classroom implementation still needs proof.

column1: Why is the electricity metering promise rated broken despite the Presidential Metering Initiative?
column2: Metering got funding (an initial ₦120bn tranche in 2024), but there is no evidence all connections are metered, so the universal promise is unmet.

column1: Why is fuel subsidy removal rated "kept"?
column2: It was a discrete policy action implemented in May 2023; its welfare impact is a separate question.

column1: What is the difference between "Not demonstrated" and "not done"?
column2: Not demonstrated means public evidence is insufficient; the work may exist but is unproven.

column1: Give an example of a promise that is "not yet due".
column2: Raising cultivated arable land from 35% to 65% (target May 2027) or five-minute access to potable water by 2030.

column1: Give an example of a manifesto promise whose deadline passed without evidence of delivery.
column2: One million ICT jobs within 24 months (deadline 29 May 2025); 3MTT training launched, but training is not proof of jobs.

column1: What progress exists on the promise to recruit more security personnel?
column2: A November 2025 order to recruit 20,000 police officers plus authorised military and DSS recruitment; recruitment is not yet proof of deployment.

column1: Give an example of MSME or creative-economy support cited as progress.
column2: The iDICE programme, a $170.6 million fund for technology start-ups and creative businesses.

column1: How should a caller respond to "Only 20.8% of promises were kept"?
column2: Acknowledge it as a third-party assessment, then discuss verified achievements and gaps promise by promise; never call the report fake or claim all promises are fulfilled.

column1: What is the core rule for answering criticism about promises?
column2: Answer the promise actually made, not a related programme; for example, metering funds do not prove every customer has a meter.

column1: “He only kept 20% of his promises.”
column2: That's one group's assessment, AdvoKC, and it's worth reading in full: another 41% of promises show real progress but aren't finished. Education scored best: student loans, a new school curriculum and fewer university strikes. Some promises, like ending kidnapping, haven't been met, and I won't pretend they have.
column3: AdvoKC BAT-O-METER (June 2026): 11 kept, 22 compromised, 20 broken of 53. Never call the report fake.

column1: “He promised to revive Ajaokuta and finish the railways. Nothing.”
column2: Those promises are behind, and that's fair criticism. Some rail work is under way, like Kaduna-Kano, but construction isn't completion. The campaign should show clear timelines for both, not just announcements.
column3: AdvoKC rates both broken. Never say Ajaokuta is revived without production evidence.

column1: Give examples of manifesto targets that are not yet due.
column2: Raising cultivated farmland from 35% to 65% (due May 2027) and five-minute access to clean water (due 2030). Not being complete yet is not automatically a failure.
column3: Also: "not demonstrated" (no public evidence yet) is not the same as "not done".

column1: What did AdvoKC rate as kept?
column2: 11 promises, including student loans, the new national curriculum, reduced ASUU strike disruption and fuel subsidy removal (as a policy action).
column3: Economy: 8 of 31 kept. Education: 3 of 4 kept.
